chapter_theme: The battle of the champions: the danava Arikethanan is cut down by Sarthulakan, Dhumaketu boasts and falls to the Vidyadhara king's younger brother, and Azhalvegan and Devasenan trade taunts.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark-hued youth, the groom
the danava of the discus-lord's kin who is killed
the discus-lord's kin who comes after Arikethanan
the Vidyadhara side and its kings
the Vidyadhara king's younger brother, the blazing chariot lord
the spear-skilled youth who comes in after Dhumaketu's fall
the lord of kings who goes out against Azhalvegan

1307.reading: The youth draws his great bow and looses an arrow that lands in a warrior's mouth, so that a man named Pukazh Varasenan falls on the field, and then a danava of the foe steps out among them.
1307.nuance: The youth is not named; he is taken to be Tivittan from the later epithet in 1319, and the clause naming the fallen man and the danava is hard to parse.
1307.event: A warrior of the youth's side shoots down one enemy, and a danava comes out in his place.

1308.reading: A danava wears garlands of entrails and skulls, hangs infants' heads in his ears, and strides among cut-off elephant trunks with a flaming trident.
1308.nuance: The verse never names him; 1312 gives the name Arikethanan to the man who comes at this point, so the identification rests on that.
1308.event: The danava prowls the field, hung with gore.

1309.reading: Blood is his wine and his hands the cup, enemy bodies his meat; those behind him snap their fingers and whistle, saying that no one in this world will fail to think of such food.
1309.event: The danava advances in blood-lust with followers behind him.

1310.reading: Elephant tusks he tears out, enemy soldiers he drinks dry with his bright sword, and none who meets him unaware escapes.
1310.event: The danava slaughters soldiers and elephants as he comes.

1311.reading: Black as night, flame-like, with a lion's roar, he kicks the chariots and horses of the field so that they burst like popped grain; the poet calls this the splendour of his coming.
1311.event: The danava smashes chariots and horses as he advances.

1312.reading: The man named Arikethanan, the discus-lord's Death, tells himself that he has fought many armies and asks what use this poor army is as a match, and so comes on.
1312.nuance: The text calls him the discus-lord's தமன், kin, and compares him to Yama; the boast in the second half is his own thought or speech.
1312.event: Arikethanan, kin of the discus-lord, comes to the fight scorning the opposing army.

1313.reading: Sarthulakan, joyful in battle though not drunk, draws his sword and meets the danava with the cry that he will drink his life.
1313.event: Sarthulakan of the youth's side takes up the danava's challenge.

1314.reading: As dark as hill, cloud and night, the foe swells like a sea and then shrinks into a single point on earth; the poet calls it the splendour of battle.
1314.nuance: The verse is pure description of the two as they close.

1315.reading: The danava, with fangs like the waxing moon and shoulders like wooded hills, drives his trident into the chest of his opponent.
1315.nuance: The subject is not named; the sense depends on 1316, where the pierced man cuts back.
1315.event: Arikethanan pierces Sarthulakan's chest with his trident.

1316.reading: Pierced as he was, Sarthulakan hurls the sword and cuts the thrower in two with the very trident, the huge man falls like a mountain, and his own kin are broken.
1316.nuance: Who falls is read from the next verse, which says the man's day of life was spent.
1316.event: Sarthulakan kills Arikethanan and the discus-lord's kin lose heart.

1317.reading: His days of life spent, the fallen man lies like a hill while the discus-lord's kin on the mountain fear; then Dhumaketu, like the fire of the age's end and Death and thunder, arrives on a rutting elephant.
1317.nuance: The phrase that his days were used up lets the poet put the death in fate beside Sarthulakan's skill; the text gives both without ranking.
1317.event: Arikethanan is dead and Dhumaketu rides in to take the field.

claims.claim: a man dies when the days of his life are used up

1318.reading: Dhumaketu boasts aloud: shall he lift the mountain, split the earth, drain the sea, burn the world and eat its lives; what can bow-men and archers do, and who among the foe equals him?
1318.event: Dhumaketu boasts that no enemy equals him.

1319.reading: The young brother of the dark-hued youth's father-in-law, wearing garlands, a diamond-studded mace and a golden gem-wreath, sees him coming and goes joyfully to answer that a battle has come.
1319.nuance: Read as the king's younger brother (மாமனுக் கிளையான்), whom 1321 names as the owner of the blazing chariot; the speech opens in this verse and runs on in 1320.
1319.event: The Vidyadhara king's younger brother goes to meet Dhumaketu.

1320.reading: He answers Dhumaketu's boast clause by clause: you would lift the mountain, split the earth, drink the sea and eat lives; will you claim no one is your equal? Stand, and your match will come until you are destroyed.
1320.event: The Vidyadhara king's younger brother mocks Dhumaketu's boast.

1321.reading: Dhumaketu hears him, laughs, and says that this is the one called the lord of the blazing chariot, and asks whether he will really fight him and not shrink, and raises his mace.
1321.nuance: The title of the man he laughs at is எரியுடைத் தேரோன், which is what ties this scene to the chariot of the blazing fire in the Vidyadhara king's younger brother.
1321.event: Dhumaketu mocks him and takes up his mace.

1322.reading: The man answers that Dhumaketu was right to scorn him, and asks if any who stood against him ever stood speaking as loudly; they rise to the fight and the world shakes and the kings stand clear.
1322.event: The two rise and join battle; the other kings stand aside.

1323.reading: The directions roar, the earth shakes, the seas churn, darkness covers the sky and hills roll; the two strike with mace and shield and sweat though their hearts burn, circling in the sky.
1323.event: The duel of the two shakes the world.

1324.reading: To all who look, their forms are hard to see; mace, ring and garland, jewels and noise fill the eight quarters, the ground and the dark sky, the mountains tremble and even Death shivers.
1324.nuance: The verse describes the fighting rather than telling an act.

1325.reading: One of the fighters, black as a great mountain, falls rolling from the fray with his gold ear-stud and garland shattered, and the crowned kings say, will even Dhumaketu lose to one man, and lose their pride.
1325.nuance: Read as Dhumaketu's fall, from the kings' reaction naming him.
1325.event: Dhumaketu is struck down; the kings who stood with him are dismayed.

1326.reading: The mighty fall, banners drop and flames of the spear remain; the kings ask what they gain by standing and bid him rise, and a young man comes quickly.
1326.nuance: The wording is difficult; the speakers are the discus-lord's kings and the arriving youth is identified as Azhalvegan from 1328.
1326.event: After Dhumaketu's fall another young warrior is sent in.

1327.reading: He comes with a spear, wearing flowered garlands, with scent in his locks and gems swinging at his ears, and the poet asks what is the resolve of this man.

1328.reading: Speaking of the spear-skilled Azhalvegan, he says: if it is he, let it be; let the young ones stand aside and let him face me; Devasenan, lord of kings, goes red before him.
1328.nuance: The speaker of the opening is not named; Devasenan's words fit because he then goes out.

1329.reading: Azhalvegan says to him: you live scorning me even on the hill and give nothing to men; you will fight on earth; when I win and take your head I will uproot your whole clan.
1329.event: Azhalvegan threatens Devasenan with the destruction of his line.

1330.reading: Devasenan answers with the same words turned back, calls Azhalvegan's boast false, asks if this is his manhood, and meets him spear to spear.
1330.nuance: The reply repeats the opening of 1329 almost word for word, so the exchange is a mirror.
1330.event: Devasenan returns the taunt and the two fight.

1331.reading: The poet says no one could tell, except at the day's end, the ways of the sword and spear, the turns of the shoulders, the war-talk and the sounds of the fighters.
1331.nuance: The narrator breaks off to say the fight cannot be fully described.

links.note: The danava pierces Sarthulakan in 1315, and in 1316 the pierced man cuts him down with the trident.
links.teaches: The wound does not decide the duel; the wounded man's counter-stroke decides it, so the pair shows the fight reversed in one verse.

links.note: The pierced Sarthulakan fights on and kills the thrower, as in the Kural's warrior who sends his spear off and smiles at the one in his own body.
links.teaches: The poem makes the Kural's warrior who smiles at a spear in his body into a man who turns the wound into a weapon.

gains.a: 1316 gains a norm that treats a wound received in the fight as a mark of the warrior, not a loss
gains.b: Kural 774 gains an actual wounded fighter who turns the thrown trident on its thrower, not only a smile

links.note: Dhumaketu is likened to the Death of the age's end; Tirumular says the Lord's thinkers are beyond Death's messengers.
links.teaches: The war poem sets Death above all fighters, while Tirumular sets one who thinks of the Lord above Death.

gains.a: 1317 gains a view in which the Death its hero resembles can be turned back
gains.b: Tirumanthiram 176 gains the epic's warrior who becomes Death's own image on the field

links.note: Dhumaketu's boast in 1318 is repeated clause by clause and turned back by the younger king in 1320.
links.teaches: The answer uses the boaster's own clauses to cut him down, so the boast is shown to be what ruins him.

links.note: Dhumaketu's boast of lifting hills and drinking the sea is the kind of word the Naladiyar says the excellent never speak.
links.teaches: The epic gives the Naladiyar's rule a case in which the boast comes just before a fall.

gains.a: 1318 gains a standard by which its hero's boast marks him as the lesser man
gains.b: Naladiyar 346 gains a warrior's boast whose price is paid in the next verses

links.note: The younger king's promise that Dhumaketu's match will come is kept in 1325 when Dhumaketu rolls from the field.
links.teaches: The prediction made in the taunt is fulfilled in a few verses.
Giving the same words to both fighters leaves the taunt itself as the thing the poet shows, with neither side ahead.

source_issues: Verses 1307, 1317 to 1331 were printed as eight half-lines and joined into four.
Verse 1313 had a stray pulli removed.
The speakers of 1319 to 1322 and 1328 to 1330 are inferred from the epithets in the text, and the fallen man in 1325 is read from the kings' reaction.
